title: Omissive Causation or the Failure to Act
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article introduces the concept of omissive causation — negative outcomes caused by inaction rather than action — and argues that leaders systematically underweight it compared to more visible cause-and-effect relationships. It offers everyday examples (an unwatered plant dying, withheld feedback producing underperformance) to make the abstract concept concrete, then pivots to a psychological wrinkle: when leaders are surprised by the consequences of someone's inaction, they tend to react more harshly and attribute worse motives (negligence, cowardice) than they would to an equivalent failure caused by an active choice. The piece's practical recommendation is to actively scan for causal relationships rooted in inaction, not just action, as part of ordinary strategic thinking.
points: The essay names a specific asymmetry in leader psychology: failures of omission trigger harsher, more punitive attributions than equivalent failures of commission.
It supplies a memorable definitional anchor (omissive causation) that gives leaders vocabulary for a pattern they likely already sense but haven't named.
The everyday examples (unwatered plants, withheld feedback) ground an abstract causal concept in immediately recognizable scenarios.
Its practical takeaway is procedural: build scanning for inaction into the same observational habit leaders already use for action-based cause and effect.
quotes: What leaders generally underestimate in this learning process are the negative effects of inaction. Formally called omissive causation, the absence of an event that causes an effect is nearly as common as its sibling but is often overlooked until it is too late.
Examples of omissive causation are everywhere: When we fail to water a plant, it dies. When we choose not to give people candid feedback, they underperform.
The reasons leaders attribute to others when they are surprised by omissive causation are not pretty and include negligence, irresponsibility, laziness, and even cowardice.
Not surprisingly, leaders who are startled to learn of a failure to act are less forgiving and more punitive to those they deem responsible.
Sometimes it is what we don’t do that has the biggest impact on the outcomes we create.
